01_annual_trend_coverage: How do reported counts and coverage change annually?
Sum known selected New outbreaks by Year; percentage change uses consecutive observed years without filling missing counts.
2011 peaks at 688,141; Iran / Paenibacillus larvae (American foulbrood) contributes 66.7% of that total.
Use the peak and coverage changes to choose periods for disease-specific review.
Unknown groups contribute no numeric count; counts may be partial. Country numbers do not measure complete reporting or livestock exposure.
02_semester_trend: When do six-month reported counts peak?
Sum by explicit reporting semester; add a trailing mean of four observed semesters.
2024 contains 2 semester labels; country coverage is half 1: 129, half 2: 126.
Half-year variation can guide finer data requests.
These are reporting-period counts; precise onset/report dates and monthly seasonality are unavailable. A trailing mean is descriptive.
03_top_disease_trends: Are high-count diseases stable or dominated by spikes?
Use unmerged top ten source labels and separate annual y-axis scales; missing years remain gaps.
The top ten labels account for 54.0% of known counts. See exported series for exact peaks.
Separate scales reveal shapes obscured by the global total.
Disease definitions change over time; no merged HPAI or tuberculosis continuity is assumed. Counts across disease definitions may not represent unique biological events.
04_disease_region_ranking: Which diseases and regions contribute most known counts?
Sum known counts after verified duplication removal, subtype-preserving selection and category priority.
Paenibacillus larvae (American foulbrood) and Middle East lead their rankings.
Prioritise these contributors for source verification and targeted analysis.
Reported counts reflect reporting and heterogeneous outbreak definitions, not underlying risk; bee animal units must not be confused with outbreak counts.
05_region_trends: Do regions show different temporal patterns?
Annual regional sums with missing region-years left as gaps.
The largest cumulative regional share is Middle East (25.0%).
Review regional peaks separately rather than infer a single global trajectory.
Country participation and administrative coverage vary; regional totals lack population denominators.
06_disease_region_heatmap: Known disease-region counts on log10(count+1); blanks are unobserved, explicit zero remains zero.
Paenibacillus larvae (American foulbrood) is the highest-count source disease label overall.
Log colour supports comparison across large differences in scale.
Colour does not indicate adjusted risk or establish disease absence in blank cells.
07_region_composition: How does the disease mix differ across regions?
Shares of each regional known-count total: top ten labels plus all other observed disease labels.
Top ten labels contribute 54.0% globally; regional mixes are in disease_region.csv.
Composition is useful for choosing regional disease case studies.
Shares condition on known counts. Blank combinations add no observed contribution; this does not impute disease absence.
08_disease_year_heatmap: Which high-count diseases have abrupt peaks or changing label coverage?
Log10 annual sums for unchanged top source labels, with gaps retained.
The global count peak is 2011; each disease may peak in a different year.
Compare concentrated spikes with sustained patterns before selecting a model.
Renamed or newly introduced labels may create structural gaps; missing data are not zero.
09_half_year_patterns: Pool known counts by Jan–Jun and Jul–Dec for top diseases; show semester-year totals separately.
Bluetongue has 92.7% of known counts in Jul–Dec. Shares describe reporting periods, not monthly onset seasonality.
Use these contrasts to design region-specific seasonal follow-up.
Pooled hemispheres, reporting lag, one-off peaks, and incomplete coverage can mimic seasonality. No monthly or significance claim is supported.
10_exploratory_anomalies: Which recent semester counts depart from their historical same-half baseline?

Prior five consecutive same-half years only; log1p(known counts / disease-specific observed countries), median and scaled MAD; screen positive robust scores >3.5. Skip incomplete-count periods and zero MAD.

467 flags among 6425 eligible comparisons. The figure prioritises selected diseases with at least three observed countries and 50 known counts, one region per disease. For Asia/FMD 2022 half 1, observed counts per reporting country are 2,488.8 versus historical median 85.5 (29.1×); Indonesia contributes 32,078 known counts.
Use flags as a reproducible triage list for source review; five points are too few for calibrated tail probabilities.
No p-values, false-positive calibration, causal inference or forecast validation. Country composition may change, denominator is a reporting proxy, and excluded ambiguous groups can lower counts.
11_country_ranking: Are known counts concentrated in a few countries?
Rank cumulative known country counts after regional de-duplication.
The top five countries account for 41.0%.
No livestock denominators, comparable surveillance capacity or uniform outbreak definition.
12_priority_disease_regions: Which regions drive changes in selected diseases?
Separate annual regional sums for six observed source disease labels; HPAI categories remain separate; no absent years are filled.

Peak observed global years: African swine fever: 2021 (15,477); Foot and mouth disease: 2022 (62,180); Lumpy skin disease: 2022 (61,433); Bluetongue: 2008 (34,276); HPAI (poultry): 2022 (4,118); HPAI (non-poultry, 2017–): 2022 (5,014).
These peaks identify focused disease-region case studies for Challenge 6.
Coverage and source definitions change; the non-poultry HPAI label begins in 2017 and cannot be compared with an invented pre-2017 zero baseline.
